t: Middle Persian, the language of Persia proper, became the prestige and literary language of the Sasanian Empire, used even by non-Persian Iranians, and stayed a prestige language for some time after the empire fell.

It had shed most of Old Persian’s case endings, using prepositions and compound tenses instead, and in its past tenses it treated the doer of an action like a by-phrase, an ergative pattern that New Persian gave up.

Almost all its literature is Zoroastrian, written mostly in the 9th to 11th centuries in Book Pahlavi, when the language had long ceased to be spoken; so the script’s name, Pahlavi, came to mean the language itself.
dyk: Pahlavi scribes wrote many Persian words as Aramaic ones, about a thousand in Book Pahlavi: “me” was written LY, Aramaic for “to me”, but read aloud as the Persian man, and “foot” was written as Aramaic for “his foot” and read pāy.
ev: The fall of the Achaemenid Empire opens the Middle period of the Iranian languages
Coins issued in the province of Pars carry legends in early Pahlavi
The Sasanians, native speakers of Middle Persian, take power from the Parthian Arsacids, and Middle Persian becomes the prestige language of the state
The prophet Mani writes the Šābuhragān in Middle Persian in a script of his own making
The earliest Zoroastrian texts in Middle Persian are probably written down, codifying an older oral tradition
The Arabs overthrow the Sasanians, and Middle Persian begins to evolve rapidly into New Persian
Most surviving Zoroastrian Middle Persian texts are written, long after the language has ceased to be spoken
Copyists make most of the manuscripts through which Middle Persian texts survive

f.family: Indo-European; Iranian, a Western Middle Iranian language; descended from Old Persian, the language of the Achaemenid Empire, and the ancestor of New Persian, Achomi and Luri
f.script: abjads (scripts of consonants) from Imperial Aramaic: the Pahlavi scripts, full of Aramaic word-signs, in early Pahlavi on coins of Pars (2nd century BCE to 3rd century CE), Inscriptional Pahlavi (3rd–4th centuries CE), Psalter Pahlavi (6th–8th centuries) and Book Pahlavi (from the 5th century); the Manichaean script of the prophet Mani (216–274); later Pazand (the Avestan alphabet) and Pārsī (the Perso-Arabic script)
f.earliest: early Pahlavi legends on the coins of the province of Pars from the 2nd century BCE; the Sasanian royal inscriptions of the 3rd–4th centuries CE, among them the multilingual inscription of Shapur I and Kartir’s inscription on the Ka'ba-ye Zartosht; Mani’s Šābuhragān in the 3rd century
f.status: extinct: the spoken language evolved into New Persian after the 7th century, and Zoroastrian writing in it went on into the 9th–11th centuries; its descendants are New Persian (official in Iran, in Afghanistan as Dari and in Tajikistan as Tajik), Achomi and Luri
